problems.title: Quantifiers in an arbitrary open union
problems.objective: Use one membership witness instead of seeking a nonexistent common radius.
problems.statement: Let $\{U_i:i\in I\}$ be open subsets of $\mathbb R$. Prove that $\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i$ is open, including $I=\varnothing$, and explain why the proof needs neither a radius common to all $U_i$ nor a minimum over $I$.
permittedResults: The pointwise definition of openness in $\mathbb R$.
Membership in an indexed union is existential.
The empty set is open.
problems.strategy: If $x$ lies in the union, unpack that membership to select one index $i_0$ with $x\in U_{i_0}$. Next, use only the radius supplied by openness of $U_{i_0}$; no radius from any other set is relevant. Finally, handle $I=\varnothing$ separately and identify the union as empty.
hints: Unpack $x\in\bigcup_iU_i$ to obtain one witness $i_0$ with $x\in U_{i_0}$.
Use the radius for $U_{i_0}$ alone to place a ball inside the full union.
When $I=\varnothing$, the union is $\varnothing$, so there is no point at which a radius must be chosen.
problems.solution: Suppose $x\in\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i$. By the meaning of union membership, some $i_0\in I$ satisfies $x\in U_{i_0}$. Since $U_{i_0}$ is open, there is $r>0$ with $B(x,r)\subseteq U_{i_0}\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i$. Thus the union is open. The radius may depend on both $x$ and its witness $i_0$; no minimum over all indices is needed. If $I=\varnothing$, the union is $\varnothing$, which is open vacuously.
rubricCriteria: Unpacks union membership to obtain one index $i_0$ containing the chosen point.
Uses the radius for $U_{i_0}$ alone and explains why no common or minimum radius is required.
Handles the empty index set and concludes that the arbitrary union is open.

problems.objective: Construct one neighborhood radius and isolate exactly where finiteness is used.
problems.statement: Let $J$ be finite and let $U_j\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open for every $j\in J$. Prove $\bigcap_{j\in J}U_j$ is open by constructing a common radius at each point, and treat $J=\varnothing$ explicitly.

A nonempty finite set of positive real numbers has a positive minimum.
The intersection of an empty family of subsets of $\mathbb R$ is $\mathbb R$.
problems.strategy: If $J=\varnothing$, identify the intersection with $\mathbb R$. Otherwise, for $x$ in the intersection choose $r_j>0$ with $B(x,r_j)\subseteq U_j$. Finally, take the positive minimum of this nonempty finite family and use it for every $j$.

For nonempty finite $J$ and $x$ in the intersection, choose one positive radius $r_j$ for each $j$.
Set $r=\min_{j\in J}r_j$ and verify $B(x,r)\subseteq U_j$ for every $j$.
problems.solution: If $J=\varnothing$, then $\bigcap_{j\in J}U_j=\mathbb R$, which is open. Now suppose $J$ is nonempty and finite. problems.title: Closure of an oscillatory graph
problems.objective: Determine every boundary fiber created by oscillation near a missing endpoint.
problems.statement: Let $E=\{(x,\sin(1/x)):0<x\le1\}\subseteq\mathbb R^2$. Prove $$\overline E=E\cup\bigl(\{0\}\times[-1,1]\bigr).$$
permittedResults: Sequential characterization of closure in $\mathbb R^2$.
Continuity of $x\mapsto\sin(1/x)$ on $(0,\infty)$.
For every $y\in[-1,1]$, there is $\theta\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ with $\sin\theta=y$.
problems.strategy: Prove both inclusions sequentially. To create a prescribed point $(0,y)$, choose a phase $\theta$ with $\sin\theta=y$ and set $x_n=1/(\theta+2\pi n)$ for sufficiently large $n$. To exclude other points, analyze any convergent sequence from the graph according to whether its first-coordinate limit is positive or zero.
hints: For $y\in[-1,1]$, choose $\theta$ with $\sin\theta=y$ and make $1/x_n=\theta+2\pi n$.
If graph points $(x_n,\sin(1/x_n))$ converge and $x_n\to x>0$, use continuity to identify the second-coordinate limit.
If $x_n\to0$, use $-1\le\sin(1/x_n)\le1$ and closedness of $[-1,1]$ to restrict the second-coordinate limit.
problems.solution: Every point of $E$ belongs to $\overline E$. Now fix $y\in[-1,1]$ and choose $\theta\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ with $\sin\theta=y$. For all sufficiently large $n$, set $x_n=1/(\theta+2\pi n)>0$. Then $x_n\to0$ and periodicity gives $\sin(1/x_n)=\sin(\theta+2\pi n)=y$, so $(x_n,\sin(1/x_n))\to(0,y)$. Hence the proposed right-hand side lies in $\overline E$. Conversely, suppose $(x_n,\sin(1/x_n))\in E$ converges to $(x,y)$. Since $0<x_n\le1$, one has $0\le x\le1$. If $x>0$, continuity of $t\mapsto\sin(1/t)$ gives $y=\sin(1/x)$, so $(x,y)\in E$. If $x=0$, the inequalities $-1\le\sin(1/x_n)\le1$ pass to the limit, giving $y\in[-1,1]$. No other limit points are possible, proving the equality.
rubricCriteria: Constructs a graph sequence converging to every prescribed point of $\{0\}\times[-1,1]$.
Uses continuity to classify limits whose first coordinate is positive.
Uses the sine range to classify zero-coordinate limits and completes both set inclusions.

problems.title: An exterior point has a positive gap from a compact set
problems.objective: Turn compactness into a quantitative neighborhood disjoint from the set.
problems.statement: Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R$ be nonempty and compact, and let $x\notin K$. Prove there is $r>0$ such that $B(x,r)\cap K=\varnothing$. Then prove $\inf\{|x-y|:y\in K\}>0$.
permittedResults: The extreme value theorem on nonempty compact sets.
The function $y\mapsto|x-y|$ is continuous.
The triangle inequality.
problems.strategy: Apply the extreme value theorem to the continuous function $y\mapsto|x-y|$ on $K$. Its minimum is attained at some $y_0\in K$ and is positive because $x\notin K$. Finally, use half that minimum as the radius of a ball about $x$ disjoint from $K$.
hints: Minimize the continuous function $g(y)=|x-y|$ over the nonempty compact set $K$.
If its attained minimum were zero, the minimizing point would equal $x$, contradicting $x\notin K$.
Use $r=|x-y_0|/2$ and the triangle inequality to exclude every point of $K$ from $B(x,r)$.
problems.solution: The function $g(y)=|x-y|$ is continuous on the nonempty compact set $K$, so it attains a minimum $m=|x-y_0|$ at some $y_0\in K$. If $m=0$, then $x=y_0\in K$, contrary to hypothesis; hence $m>0$. For every $y\in K$, minimality gives $|x-y|\ge m$, so $B(x,m/2)\cap K=\varnothing$. The same inequality shows $m$ is the infimum of $\{|x-y|:y\in K\}$, and therefore that infimum is positive.
rubricCriteria: Applies compactness and continuity to obtain an attained minimum distance.
Proves the minimum is strictly positive using the exterior-point hypothesis.
Builds a disjoint ball and identifies the same positive number as the distance infimum.

commonErrors.description: Uses the invalid claim or step: Since $x\notin K$, every distance $|x-y|$ is positive, so their infimum is automatically positive.
commonErrors.consequence: Pointwise positivity does not by itself give a uniform positive lower bound.

commonErrors.description: Finds a positive minimizing distance but never uses it to construct a ball disjoint from $K$.
commonErrors.consequence: The requested exterior neighborhood remains unproved.

problems.flawedProof: Since $x\notin K$, each number $|x-y|$ with $y\in K$ is positive, so their infimum is positive. This is invalid without compactness: a set of positive numbers may have infimum zero.

problems.title: Closed rectangles are path connected
problems.objective: Construct explicit paths using convex combinations.
problems.statement: Let $R=[a,b]\times[c,d]\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, where $a\le b$ and $c\le d$. For arbitrary $p,q\in R$, prove the path $\gamma(t)=(1-t)p+tq$ remains in $R$ for $0\le t\le1$. Conclude that $R$ is path connected and therefore connected.
permittedResults: Affine maps from $[0,1]$ into $\mathbb R^2$ are continuous.
A path-connected set is connected.
Convex-combination inequalities in closed intervals.
problems.strategy: Write the coordinates of $\gamma(t)$ as convex combinations of the corresponding coordinates of $p$ and $q$. Use the interval bounds on both endpoints to keep each coordinate in its closed interval. Finally, verify continuity of $\gamma$ and invoke the implication from path connectedness to connectedness.
hints: Express each coordinate of $\gamma(t)$ as $(1-t)p_i+tq_i$.
Use $0\le t\le1$ to show a convex combination of two points of a closed interval remains in that interval.
Check that $\gamma(0)=p$, $\gamma(1)=q$, and that $\gamma$ is continuous.
problems.solution: Write $p=(p_1,p_2)$ and $q=(q_1,q_2)$. For $0\le t\le1$, both coefficients $1-t$ and $t$ are nonnegative and sum to one. Since $a\le p_1,q_1\le b$, one has $a\le(1-t)p_1+tq_1\le b$; similarly, $c\le(1-t)p_2+tq_2\le d$. Thus $\gamma(t)\in R$ for every $t\in[0,1]$. The coordinate functions of $\gamma$ are affine, hence continuous, and $\gamma(0)=p$, $\gamma(1)=q$. Therefore every two points of $R$ are joined by a path in $R$, so $R$ is path connected and consequently connected.

Uses convex-combination inequalities to prove the entire path remains in the rectangle.
Verifies endpoints and continuity, then concludes path connectedness and connectedness.

problems.title: Maximum oscillation on a compact set
problems.objective: Apply compactness on a product space to maximize pairwise output variation.
problems.statement: Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R$ be nonempty and compact, and let $f:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Prove there are $x_*,y_*\in K$ such that $|f(x)-f(y)|\le|f(x_*)-f(y_*)|$ for all $x,y\in K$.
